Receiving their testimony does not reproduce the original physical encounter, but it brings later believers into the life disclosed through it and shared within the Church.

CCC 515.

sources.label: CCC 515
sources.supports: The visible humanity of Jesus reveals the mystery of his divine person and mission.

title: Truth makes room for mercy
body:
The letter addresses believers, warning them against the claim that they have moved beyond all need of forgiveness. Denial can preserve a reassuring self-image while closing the person to the mercy they need. The Catechism uses this passage to explain why receiving forgiveness includes acknowledging fault. Such honesty differs from endlessly accusing oneself or refusing to recognise genuine growth. It is a truthful response to a God whose faithfulness makes confession possible. The next verse promises cleansing rather than humiliation, so the exposure of sin serves restored communion. A Christian community should therefore make room for repentance without turning admission of failure into permanent exclusion. The truth is healing when it allows a person to stop defending the false claim that there is nothing to forgive.

CCC 1847.

sources.label: CCC 1847
sources.supports: Receiving mercy requires honest acknowledgement of sin.

title: An advocate at our side
body:
Counsellor here carries more than the idea of someone offering advice. The title is associated with Paraclete, which the Catechism explains as one called to a person's side, an advocate or consoler. The same title is used of the Holy Spirit in John's Gospel, while Jesus is the first consoler. In this letter, it gives assurance after sin: the righteous Christ intercedes for those who need mercy. The opening purpose remains clear, that believers should not sin, so advocacy is not permission for indifference. It is the reason failure need not end in despair. The person who returns to God does not approach without help; the one who has given himself for sinners remains their living advocate with the Father.

CCC 692; CCC 2634.

sources.label: CCC 692
sources.supports: The title Paraclete names one called alongside as advocate or consoler and applies first to Jesus.

sources.label: CCC 2634
sources.supports: Christ intercedes with the Father for humanity, especially sinners.

phrase: we will see him just as he is
title: Seeing God transforms the beholder
body:
The promised future joins likeness to God with seeing him as he is. Catholic tradition calls this fulfilment the beatific vision, meaning the direct knowledge of God that brings complete happiness. The Catechism uses this verse to describe life with Christ after purification. The promise does not mean that creatures become identical with God or exhaust his mystery. It means that communion will no longer be limited by the distance and obscurity of our present condition. The verse begins with a real belonging already given, while admitting that its final form is not yet disclosed. Hope therefore includes both confidence and humility. We know whom we are being drawn towards, even though we cannot yet picture the fullness of what his presence will make of us.

CCC 1023.

sources.label: CCC 1023
sources.supports: Those perfected in grace live with Christ and behold God as he is.

title: Begin with the need before you
body:
Love becomes credible through action that answers a real need. Augustine connects this verse with the preceding example of a person who has resources but closes their heart to a hungry brother. He encourages hearers who feel unable to imagine heroic self-sacrifice: begin by sharing what you can now, and let charity grow. The insight is both demanding and hopeful. Great declarations about willingness to die for others can conceal refusal to offer ordinary help today. Yet the absence of heroic strength need not become an excuse for doing nothing. Love can be nourished through concrete generosity, offered from mercy rather than display. The verse asks whether the name Christian is becoming visible in deeds, especially where another person's need has already come within our reach.

Augustine, Hom. 1 John 5.

sources.label: Augustine, Hom. 1 John 5
sources.supports: Concrete sharing with a needy neighbour is the beginning through which charity grows.

title: Love belongs to God’s own being
body:
John's statement goes beyond saying that God sometimes acts lovingly. The Catechism understands it as revealing God's own life: Father, Son and Holy Spirit are an eternal communion of love, into which human beings are invited. Love is therefore not something God had to create others in order to acquire. It belongs eternally to who he is. This gives depth to the letter's practical demand that believers love one another. Knowing God cannot remain untouched by the reality of the one known. At the same time, the sentence does not make every human desire divine simply because it is called love. Our loves need truth, healing and ordering so that they participate more faithfully in the self-giving goodness revealed by Christ.

CCC 221.

sources.label: CCC 221
sources.supports: God’s own being is the eternal love of Father, Son and Spirit, into which humanity is invited.

title: From dread towards desire
body:
The fear named here is connected with punishment and the day of judgement. Augustine describes a movement in which a person who once dreaded Christ's coming begins to desire it as love grows. The change is relational: God is increasingly known as the one loved, rather than merely the power from whom punishment must be avoided. This does not abolish reverence or make moral responsibility trivial. Nor does the verse diagnose ordinary anxiety, trauma or fearful feelings as proof that someone lacks love. Its concern is the deeper direction of spiritual growth. Charity gradually makes fidelity less like bargaining for safety and more like a child's response to being loved, allowing hope for God's presence to become stronger than the impulse to hide from it.

Augustine, Hom. 1 John 9.

sources.label: Augustine, Hom. 1 John 9
sources.supports: Growth in charity changes dread of Christ’s coming into desire for communion with him.

title: Not every failure has the same gravity
body:
John distinguishes forms of sin by their relation to spiritual life, while urging prayer for a brother who has fallen. Catholic tradition recognises here a scriptural foundation for distinguishing mortal and venial sin. The Catechism explains that mortal sin requires grave matter together with full knowledge and deliberate consent. That later formulation should not be read back as though this verse were already a complete manual for judging individual cases. The identity and situation of another person's conscience remain known fully to God. The passage takes wrongdoing seriously without making all failures identical. Its ordinary practical direction is intercession and restoration, not curiosity about who may be beyond hope. Discernment should serve repentance and healing, with humility about what we can know of another's freedom.

CCC 1854; CCC 1857.

sources.label: CCC 1854
sources.supports: Scripture and tradition distinguish sins according to their gravity.

sources.label: CCC 1857
sources.supports: Mortal sin requires grave matter, full knowledge and deliberate consent together.

title: Love has a path to follow
body:
The letter refuses to separate love from a way of living. To walk suggests repeated steps, so fidelity is more than a single generous emotion or a correct statement of belief. The Catechism describes charity as keeping Christ's commandments and abiding in his love. Obedience becomes intelligible within relationship: the commands guide the life that love seeks to give. This prevents two distortions, a rule-keeping that has lost tenderness and a claimed love that refuses every demand for truth or self-restraint. The command received from the beginning also gives continuity to the community's journey. New circumstances may require discernment, but the centre remains the same call to love God and neighbour in a manner that can be recognised through concrete conduct.

CCC 1824.

sources.label: CCC 1824
sources.supports: Charity expresses itself through keeping Christ’s commandments.

phrase: remain in the teaching of Christ
title: Progress must keep its living centre
body:
The warning follows the letter's concern about those who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Remaining in the teaching therefore means holding to the real Incarnation, not refusing every growth in understanding. The Catechism calls confession of the Son's true humanity a distinctive mark of Christian faith. A teaching that appears sophisticated but dissolves that humanity does not simply add a new insight; it changes the centre of the Gospel. The verse helps distinguish development from abandonment. Christian thought can find new language and deeper implications while remaining accountable to the Christ witnessed by the apostles. Fidelity is living continuity with him, so that the promise of communion with Father and Son is not detached from the person through whom it was revealed.

CCC 463.

sources.label: CCC 463
sources.supports: Confession of the real Incarnation is essential to Christian faith.

title: Hospitality becomes partnership in mission
body:
The people welcomed are fellow believers who were previously strangers to the host. The letter treats the practical care given to them as a faithful work, and later explains it as cooperation with the truth. Mission therefore involves more than the person who speaks publicly. It also depends on those who provide shelter, resources and encouragement. The Catechism describes Christian witness as transmission through deeds as well as words. In this setting, generosity makes room for the message to travel and for its messengers to be received as persons. The verse honours service that can remain largely invisible. A community shares responsibility for the Gospel when it supports trustworthy work beyond its familiar circle, joining practical hospitality to discernment and a generous concern for others.

CCC 2472.

sources.label: CCC 2472
sources.supports: Christian witness communicates faith through both words and actions.

phrase: loves to be first amongst them
title: When leadership becomes possession
body:
Diotrephes is criticised for a desire for pre-eminence that damages communion and hospitality. The problem is more than an unpleasant personality: ambition is shaping how the community receives others and responds to apostolic authority. The Catechism explains ecclesial ministry as service of a word and grace that belong to Christ and are given for others. A leader therefore cannot treat the Church as a territory whose boundaries exist to protect their status. The brief portrait invites sober self-examination wherever responsibility brings influence. Do we welcome another person's gifts, or feel threatened when attention is shared? True service can make room for others without losing its purpose, because its aim is the people's good rather than confirmation that the servant must always come first.

CCC 876.

sources.label: CCC 876
sources.supports: Ecclesial ministry serves a word and grace received from Christ for others.

phrase: once for all delivered to the saints
title: A received faith worth defending
body:
Jude presents the faith as an inheritance entrusted to the holy people, not a message that each influential teacher may replace. The Catechism likewise describes the apostolic deposit as belonging to the whole Church in communion with its pastors. Contending for it means fidelity to the Gospel's truth and moral demands. The language should not be used to bless aggression or make every disagreement a battle over orthodoxy. Jude's concern is teaching that distorts the community's life and misuses grace. The once-for-all gift can be understood more deeply through time, while remaining the same faith received from Christ through the apostles. Its defence is most credible when accurate teaching, humility and holy conduct remain joined, so that the manner of witness does not betray its content.

CCC 84.

sources.label: CCC 84
sources.supports: The apostolic deposit belongs to the whole Church in communion with its pastors.

title: An inherited story within inspired Scripture
body:
This episode is not narrated in the books of Moses themselves. The Catholic Encyclopedia discusses ancient Christian references connecting it with a tradition about Moses' departure, while acknowledging that Jude may have known the story through Jewish tradition. Using such material does not mean that every work associated with it has thereby become canonical Scripture. An inspired author can draw upon material familiar to readers for a particular argument without endorsing all that might accompany it. Here the point is Michael's restraint: even an archangel does not make arrogant abuse his method, but entrusts rebuke to the Lord. The passage therefore illuminates both Jude's literary world and his moral purpose, warning against the presumption of teachers whose confidence has become contemptuous speech.

CE, Epistle of St. Jude.

sources.label: CE, Epistle of St. Jude
sources.locator: Difficulties arising from the text, discussion of verse 9
sources.supports: Jude’s use of the Moses tradition does not canonise the whole associated work.

title: Defending faith includes being formed by it
body:
After warning against destructive teaching, Jude turns towards the positive work of building a faithful life. Prayer in the Spirit is part of that construction, not an optional pause from the supposedly more serious task of argument. The Catechism explains that the Spirit already draws us towards Christ whenever we begin to pray and teaches us along the way. The phrase therefore need not refer only to unusual experiences or a special style of speech. It concerns prayer made receptive to the Spirit's action, within the faith the community has received. Jude's instruction restores proportion: a person can become skilled at identifying errors while neglecting communion with God. The faith is guarded fruitfully when it is also inhabited through prayer, love and patient hope.

CCC 2670.

sources.label: CCC 2670
sources.supports: The Holy Spirit initiates and guides prayer towards Christ.

title: Discernment should preserve mercy
body:
Jude's sharp warnings do not remove the need for compassion towards people caught in confusion or danger. The verse asks for discrimination in response, so that concern for truth does not flatten every person into the same hostile category. The Catechism's account of the ministry of reconciliation offers a related pastoral principle: truth should be joined to sensitivity, patience and the desire for healing. That is an application of the wider Catholic tradition, not a claim that Jude is directly describing sacramental confession here. The common insight is that restoring a person requires attention to their actual condition. Someone wavering may need patient explanation and reassurance, while another situation calls for firmer intervention. In either case, the aim remains rescue and renewed communion rather than the satisfaction of condemnation.

CCC 1466.

sources.label: CCC 1466
sources.supports: Ministry of forgiveness requires truth, sensitivity and patient concern for the person.

title: An unveiling, not merely a disaster
body:
Revelation is also called Apocalypse, a word the Catholic Encyclopedia connects with the Greek verb meaning to reveal. Its basic sense is an unveiling, rather than the catastrophe often suggested by modern usage. The book seeks to disclose the meaning of events in relation to Christ, especially where visible power seems to belong to forces opposed to him. Its dramatic images therefore need to be read as visionary language, drawing deeply upon earlier Scripture. They are not automatically a sequence of predictions that can be matched mechanically with today's headlines. The opening also identifies the intended recipients as servants: understanding is meant to support faithful living. The reader is invited to see more deeply so that worship, courage and perseverance become possible within the world as it is.

CE, Apocalypse.

sources.label: CE, Apocalypse
sources.locator: opening definition and description of literary form
sources.supports: Apocalypse derives from a verb meaning reveal and belongs to visionary literature about final realities.

title: Christ stands among real churches
body:
The vision's lamp stands are explained later in the chapter as churches, and the following verses place the risen Christ among them. Victorinus reads the scene in that ecclesial sense, seeing the Lord present in the midst of his communities. The setting matters because Revelation soon addresses their particular strengths and failures. Heavenly vision does not bypass ordinary church life; it reveals the one to whom that life belongs. A lamp stand bears light rather than producing its own ultimate source. The image can therefore encourage communities that feel small while also challenging self-importance. Their vocation is to make Christ's light visible, receiving his consolation and correction together. His presence among them is a gift, not a guarantee that every part of their conduct already reflects him.

Victorinus, Apocalypse 1.

sources.label: Victorinus, Apocalypse 1
sources.supports: Victorinus reads Christ among the lamp stands as his presence among the churches.

title: Correctness can lose its heart
body:
The church at Ephesus has been praised for endurance and discernment, yet those achievements do not settle the question of its fidelity. Love has weakened at the centre. The Catechism teaches that gifts, service and even impressive virtues fail to attain their proper purpose without charity. This gives the warning its force: a community can become skilled at identifying falsehood while growing cold towards God and neighbour. First love need not mean recovering the emotional intensity of an earlier stage. It means returning to the living relationship from which faithful action should flow. The next verse calls for concrete repentance and renewed works. The remedy is therefore neither nostalgia nor abandoning discernment, but allowing truth and service to be animated again by love.

CCC 1826.

sources.label: CCC 1826
sources.supports: Without charity, knowledge and extraordinary gifts fail to achieve their proper purpose.

title: Nourishment for the faithful journey
body:
Manna recalls God's food for a people travelling through the wilderness. Revelation takes that memory into a promise for those who remain faithful under pressure. The Catechism explains the Christian typology in which desert manna points towards the Eucharist, the true bread from heaven. Read within that tradition, the hidden food suggests a life sustained by God's gift even when the world cannot recognise its source. This is a spiritual and sacramental reading, not a claim that every detail of the promise has only one possible meaning. Its strength lies in the continuity of divine care: the God who fed Israel continues to nourish his people towards fulfilment in Christ. Faithfulness is demanding, but the traveller is not expected to make the entire journey on self-produced strength.

CCC 1094.

sources.label: CCC 1094
sources.supports: Old Testament manna prefigures Christ as the true bread from heaven.

phrase: I stand at the door and knock
title: The initiative of an excluded guest
body:
The invitation is addressed to a church being sharply corrected, which makes its tenderness all the more striking. Christ seeks renewed fellowship with people whose self-satisfaction has left him outside their attention. The Catechism describes prayer as beginning in God's prior desire to meet us: our thirst is answered by a love already seeking relationship. The door image makes room for a genuine response. Christ's approach does not make repentance unnecessary, but it gives repentance the form of welcome rather than an attempt to earn his first interest. The promised meal expresses communion restored. The verse can therefore be prayed personally and communally, asking where familiar religious activity has become closed to the very Lord whose presence it is meant to receive.

CCC 2560.

sources.label: CCC 2560
sources.supports: Prayer begins in Christ’s prior desire to meet the person who seeks him.

title: Worship joins a larger song
body:
The repeated praise places God's holiness at the centre of the heavenly vision. The living creatures do not merely decorate a fantastic scene; the Catechism reads them as representing creation within the service of divine praise. It also teaches that the Church's sacramental celebrations participate in this heavenly liturgy. Earthly worship therefore belongs to a communion larger than the people immediately visible in a room. The vision can correct an overly narrow question about whether worship currently feels stimulating or successful. Its deepest purpose is recognition of the God who is worthy of praise. Repetition here expresses inexhaustible attention rather than a shortage of ideas, inviting the worshipper to let reverence and gratitude become more stable than the changing appetite for novelty.

CCC 1138; CCC 1139.

sources.label: CCC 1138
sources.supports: Revelation portrays creation, the saints and Mary within the praise of heaven.

sources.label: CCC 1139
sources.supports: The Church’s sacramental celebrations participate in the heavenly liturgy.

title: The slain one is alive
body:
The Lamb is both marked by slaughter and standing alive. Revelation holds crucifixion and resurrection together in one image, refusing to make victory a forgetting of self-giving love. The Catechism identifies this Lamb as Christ crucified and risen, the high priest at the centre of the true sanctuary. His wounds do not disqualify him from glory; they disclose the character of his triumph. This changes how the book's language of power should be heard. The one worthy to unveil history is not simply the strongest creature in a contest of force, but the saviour who has given himself. Christian hope can therefore look towards a victory whose deepest form remains love, even when the surrounding visions portray judgement with overwhelming dramatic intensity.

CCC 1137.

sources.label: CCC 1137
sources.supports: The slain yet standing Lamb is the crucified and risen Christ at the centre of heavenly worship.

title: Prayer belongs within heavenly communion
body:
The prayers are pictured as incense held within the worship surrounding the Lamb. What may seem fragile or unnoticed on earth has a place in the heavenly scene. The Catechism's teaching on the saints' intercession gives a Catholic framework for this communion: those united with Christ continue to care for the Church and pray through his unique mediation. The image does not make prayer a material substance that must be transported by a heavenly mechanism. It makes its value visible through the familiar sign of fragrant offering. Nor are the saints rival centres of divine power. Their concern belongs within the Lamb's own saving work, so that asking their prayers expresses the shared life of Christ's body rather than a departure from trust in him.

CCC 956.

sources.label: CCC 956
sources.supports: The saints in heaven intercede for the Church through the one mediator, Christ.

phrase: the souls of those who had been killed
title: The victims have not disappeared
body:
The martyrs are present before God, though earthly power has silenced their voices. Their place beneath the altar joins their witness to sacrificial worship and gives their deaths a significance their persecutors cannot control. The Catechism describes martyrdom as supreme witness to Christ, sustained by love and fortitude even through death. It is not the pursuit of suffering for its own sake, nor violence committed in God's name. The following cry for justice also shows that heavenly hope does not require treating wrongdoing as insignificant. The vision remembers the victims and places their cause before God. For a threatened community, that remembrance offers courage: faithfulness is not erased when it appears defeated, and the final truth of a life does not belong to those who killed it.

CCC 2473.

sources.label: CCC 2473
sources.supports: Martyrdom is loving witness to Christ sustained even through death.

title: Unity without a single human tribe
body:
The multitude is united before the Lamb while still described through peoples, languages and nations. Salvation does not appear as the triumph of one ethnic group absorbing all others. The Catechism uses this vision when explaining the Church as a sign and instrument of humanity's unity in communion with God. That unity has already begun, yet awaits its full realisation. The image therefore both consoles and judges the present Church. Every genuine crossing of prejudice can anticipate the promise, while contempt for another people contradicts it. The multitude cannot be counted by the seer, which enlarges hope beyond familiar boundaries. The reader is invited to recognise that the family gathered by the Lamb is wider than any community's current experience or preferred cultural form.

CCC 775.

sources.label: CCC 775
sources.supports: The Church is a sign and instrument of humanity’s unity in communion with God.

title: A pause before the mystery
body:
After the intensity of the seals, silence interrupts the vision. Victorinus interprets it as a beginning of everlasting rest, while noticing that it is only partial because the narrative continues. His reading is an early spiritual interpretation, not a timetable by which heaven's half-hour can be calculated on earth. The pause can also invite the reader into reverence before what exceeds explanation. The Catechism describes adoration as including respectful silence in the presence of God's greatness. Such silence is not emptiness or indifference. It is a way of receiving without immediately taking possession through speech. Within a book full of sound and movement, the stillness reminds us that revelation calls for attention and worship as well as interpretation.

Victorinus, Apocalypse 8; CCC 2628.

sources.label: Victorinus, Apocalypse 8
sources.supports: Victorinus reads the silence as a partial anticipation of everlasting rest.

sources.label: CCC 2628
sources.supports: Adoration includes reverent silence before God’s greatness.

phrase: a woman clothed with the sun
title: One image with a communal and Marian depth
body:
The woman gives birth to the Messiah and is opposed by the dragon, so her story gathers together the people through whom he comes and those who belong to him. Victorinus reads her as the ancient community of patriarchs, prophets, saints and apostles awaiting Christ. Catholic tradition also recognises a Marian depth, reflected in the Catechism's inclusion of the Mother of God within this heavenly vision. These readings need not compete as though the symbol could refer only to an isolated individual or only to a group. Mary belongs personally within Israel and the Church, giving birth to the Messiah in history. The image can therefore express both her place and the wider people's struggle, keeping the promise of divine protection before a community facing opposition.

Victorinus, Apocalypse 12; CCC 1138.

sources.label: Victorinus, Apocalypse 12
sources.supports: Victorinus interprets the woman as the ancient people awaiting the Messiah.

sources.label: CCC 1138
sources.supports: Revelation portrays creation, the saints and Mary within the praise of heaven.

phrase: because of the word of their testimony
title: Victory through faithful witness
body:
The victory described here comes through the Lamb's blood and the believers' testimony, even when that testimony costs their lives. The pattern differs sharply from the dragon's exercise of destructive power. The Catechism explains martyrdom as witness to Christ in loving union with him, sustained by fortitude rather than the desire to harm an opponent. Revelation's conquerors are therefore not necessarily those who survive or control the public stage. Their victory is fidelity to a truth that violence cannot make them betray. This should not encourage reckless pursuit of death or diminish efforts to protect the persecuted. It gives courage when protection fails: a life freely faithful to Christ can bear fruit beyond the limits imposed by those who seek to silence it.

CCC 2473.

sources.label: CCC 2473
sources.supports: Martyrdom is loving witness to Christ sustained even through death.

title: A symbolic number needs historical care
body:
The invitation to calculate suggests that the number encodes a name rather than functioning as a free-floating magical sign. The Catholic Encyclopedia discusses the practice of assigning numerical values to letters and notes the interpretation in which Nero Caesar, written in Hebrew letters, yields 666. This is a historically grounded proposal, not a Church-defined identification that settles every detail of the vision. The article itself surveys difficulties in interpreting the book, and its older scholarship should not be treated as a final modern consensus. The useful lesson is methodological: begin with the language and political world of the first hearers before inventing connections to contemporary figures or technologies. Revelation exposes power demanding idolatrous allegiance; speculation that produces only fear can obscure that central moral challenge.

CE, Apocalypse.

sources.label: CE, Apocalypse
sources.locator: Interpretation, discussion of the beast and the number 666
sources.supports: The article explains numerical name-encoding and the proposal that Hebrew Nero Caesar yields 666.

title: Love is not left behind
body:
Rest from labour does not mean that the good done in life becomes irrelevant. The works accompany those who die in the Lord because their faithful response belongs to the person God receives. The Catechism explains the enduring worth of good works within grace: adoption into God's family makes genuine participation possible, while the merits themselves remain gifts of divine goodness. This avoids imagining heaven as a wage purchased independently of Christ. It also avoids treating earthly love as disposable once death arrives. Care offered, truth upheld and mercy practised can have a significance beyond what we presently see. The promise honours weary fidelity, assuring believers that work done in the Lord is neither forgotten nor required to continue for ever without rest.

CCC 2009.

sources.label: CCC 2009
sources.supports: Good works have enduring worth as gifts of grace within adoptive communion with God.

title: Fulfilment as covenant joy
body:
The final celebration is pictured as a wedding because salvation reaches its goal in communion. The Catechism explains the bridal image as expressing both unity and a personal relationship between Christ and the Church. The bride is loved, sanctified and cared for through the bridegroom's self-gift. She is not simply absorbed into him or treated as an object. The image therefore gathers covenant, joy and faithful response into a single celebration. It also helps interpret the preparation named in the verse: holiness is readiness for a relationship, not mere compliance with an impersonal standard. The Church's present life is directed towards this promised communion, where the love begun through grace becomes fully shared and the whole people rejoices in the Lamb's gift.

CCC 796.

sources.label: CCC 796
sources.supports: The bridal image expresses Christ’s covenant love and the Church’s personal communion with him.

title: Nothing is hidden by status
body:
The great and the small stand together before the throne. Earthly status no longer determines whose story is heard or whose actions escape attention. The Catechism explains final judgement as the unveiling of each person's relationship with God, including the full consequences of good done or left undone. The books express that complete truth; the vision need not be turned into a literal heavenly filing system. Judgement according to works also does not make grace irrelevant. It reveals what a person's response has become in life. The scene is sobering because actions matter, and hopeful because concealed faithfulness and unacknowledged harm will not remain permanently misdescribed. The final account belongs to the God who knows the whole truth beyond reputation and appearances.

CCC 1039.

sources.label: CCC 1039
sources.supports: Final judgement reveals the full truth and consequences of a person’s relationship with God.

title: God’s future answers real grief
body:
The promise is strikingly personal: God wipes tears from faces rather than merely announcing that suffering is no longer permitted. The Catechism places these words within the hope of the renewed universe where God dwells with humanity. Christian fulfilment therefore concerns the healing of lives, not escape into a state where their pain never mattered. The verse does not give us a detailed account of how every wound will be healed. It assures us that death and mourning will not define creation for ever. That hope should deepen present compassion rather than replace it with easy reassurance. To sit beside someone who weeps and to relieve suffering where possible can become a small witness to the future God promises, while leaving its complete achievement in his hands.

CCC 1044.

sources.label: CCC 1044
sources.supports: God’s final dwelling with humanity ends death, suffering and tears.

phrase: the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple
title: The sign yields to unveiled presence
body:
A city without a temple might first appear to lack its sacred centre. Revelation explains the opposite: God's presence has become so immediate that a separate sanctuary is no longer needed. The Catechism describes final fulfilment through the vision of God, the inexhaustible source of happiness, peace and communion among the redeemed. The absence of a temple is therefore not the abolition of worship but the completion of what sacred signs have served. In present life, buildings, rites and sacraments help a pilgrim people receive and respond to grace. The vision points towards communion without the present distance. Its centre remains the Almighty and the Lamb, so the city is holy through shared divine presence rather than through an isolated sacred precinct within it.

CCC 1045.

sources.label: CCC 1045
sources.supports: The redeemed community finds unbroken communion in the vision of God.

phrase: a river of water of life
title: Life flows as a gift
body:
The river comes from the throne of God and the Lamb, making divine life the source of the city's abundance. The Catechism explicitly identifies this river as a beautiful symbol of the Holy Spirit. Its wider teaching on living water explains the Spirit's action as life received from Christ and welling up towards eternity. The image gathers the Bible's waters of creation, renewal and blessing into a final gift that does not run dry. It should not be reduced to a diagram of divine relationships or a physical geography of heaven. Its theological force is generosity: the fulfilled life of the redeemed is continually received, not independently possessed. Communion with God remains living and fruitful, with the Spirit expressed as a flowing source rather than a static reward.

CCC 1137; CCC 694.

sources.label: CCC 1137
sources.supports: The river flowing from God and the Lamb is identified as a symbol of the Holy Spirit.

sources.label: CCC 694
sources.supports: Living water signifies the Spirit’s life-giving action flowing from Christ.

title: The Bible ends in desire and invitation
body:
The closing cry joins the Spirit and the Church in longing for Christ, while also inviting the thirsty to receive life freely. The Catechism relates this prayer to the petition for God's kingdom: the Church's hope becomes the appeal for the Lord to come. The two directions belong together. Awaiting Christ does not close the community against others; it makes the gift available in invitation. Nor is hope merely an attempt to leave the world behind. It desires the fulfilment of the love already at work in creation and redemption. The final emphasis on receiving freely returns us to grace. Scripture's great story concludes with a people learning to desire God's presence and to welcome others to the life they themselves can only receive as gift.

CCC 2817.

sources.label: CCC 2817
sources.supports: The prayer for the kingdom joins the Spirit and Bride’s cry for Christ to come.
